clue.text: No radio seems to enhance': matters

definitions.text: No radio seems to enhance': matters

parts.words: No radio seems to enhance': matters
parts.note: two readings: when the radio sets are switched off there is no radio, and a frame or contrast enhances a thing it shows to advantage

explanation.surface: A complaint that a radio adds nothing to the matter in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: wireless sets that are off give no radio, and to enhance something by contrast is the phrasal verb in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance by contrast is to show something off well, as a frame flatters a painting.

clue.text: His Rev's meting out penance and absolution

indicators.note: meting out means dealing out or distributing, so the letters are dealt into a new order

parts.note: the letters of Rev's, with its s

explanation.surface: A clergyman hands out penance and forgiveness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meting out' rearranges HIS REVS; to shrive is to hear confession, set penance and absolve.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest who shrives a penitent hears confession, imposes penance and grants absolution.

clue.text: Carrying everybody inside, that's the lot

indicators.note: inside says one word is placed within the other

parts.note: toting means carrying
all means everybody

explanation.surface: Someone carrying everyone declares that is the whole load.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts ALL within TOTING, after TOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Adding up a list to its sum, the point at which the whole count is reached.

clue.text: Time was in the golden age

indicators.note: in says the answer lies within the next word

explanation.surface: Wistful talk of a past golden age.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'time was' means in former days, of long ago.

parts.note: not rowdy celebrations but partisan strife, the feeling of groups within a political party

explanation.surface: Rowdy with celebratory high spirits at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party spirit' suggests festivity, but it means loyalty to a political faction.
explanation.definitionFit: Riven by internal cliques or partisan groups, as in a split political movement.

indicators.note: a recipe is a set of instructions for mixing ingredients, so the letters of the herb's name are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written: alecost is the herb costmary, once used to flavour ale

explanation.surface: Discovering a recipe that uses the herb alecost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recipe' asks for the letters of ALECOST to be mixed, like ingredients.
explanation.definitionFit: To find something is to pinpoint where it is.

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An account of some brawny men.
explanation.definitionFit: To describe something at length is to dilate on it, to speak at large.

parts.note: a jester belongs to a royal household, and at the card table the king, queen and knave picture cards are the royal household

explanation.surface: A clown at a dinner table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'table' is the card table, not a dining one: the jester is pictured as a royal card.
explanation.definitionFit: A king, queen or jack in a pack of playing cards, members of the royal household.

clue.text: Thanks to the citizen for keeping silent

parts.note: ta is British informal for thank you
cit is an old abbreviation for citizen

explanation.surface: Thanking a citizen for staying quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means unspoken or implied, from the Latin for silent.

parts.note: Hamlet calls the earth 'a ... promontory' in his 'what a piece of work is a man' speech, the same word meaning free of germs

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare reference asking how clean the earth's headland is.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet Act 2, Hamlet says 'this goodly frame the earth seems to me a sterile promontory'.
explanation.definitionFit: Free from bacteria or other living micro-organisms, and also barren.

clue.text: It is right a boy should be scolded

parts.note: Ted is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Approving that a boy has been told off.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone, an old verb akin to berate, is to scold them sharply.

explanation.surface: Pointing out a particular jewel.
explanation.definitionFit: A boil or large pimple is one sense; a rounded red garnet cut without facets is the other.

parts.note: an unsigned love card sent in February, and the song mad Ophelia sings in Hamlet offering herself as one on Saint ... day

explanation.surface: Ophelia offers an unsigned letter.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet, Act 4, Ophelia sings 'Tomorrow is Saint Valentine's day ... to be your Valentine'; such February cards are traditionally sent unsigned.
explanation.definitionFit: A card sent on 14 February to a sweetheart is customarily unsigned, an anonymous message of love.

parts.note: an Italian score direction meaning that every player in the orchestra joins in

explanation.surface: Praise for something complete in musical terms.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian direction means all performers play together, so the passage includes everyone.

parts.note: not an enlightening press clipping but a twist of newspaper used to carry a flame to a pipe or fire

explanation.surface: An informative clipping from a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Illuminating cutting' suggests an informative press clipping; it is literally a bit of paper used to light something.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin strip or twist of paper or wood used for lighting a fire or pipe.

clue.text: As a matter of fact, Lily is' coming round later anyhow

indicators.note: anyhow means in a careless, disordered way, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lily is calling in later in any case, as it happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' jumbles LILY and LATER; 'is coming round' links them.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means actually or in the strict sense, exactly as stated.

parts.note: the drink of the Greek gods on Mount Olympus was nectar, and this fruit's name grows from that word

explanation.surface: Asking what fruit grows on the gods' mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: A smooth-skinned peach variety named after the gods' drink, nectar.

clue.text: Punished for having looked after the till?

definitions.text: Punished for having looked after the till?

parts.words: Punished for having looked after the till?
parts.note: a cashier looks after a till, but the verb means dismissed from the armed forces in disgrace

explanation.surface: A shop worker penalised for minding the cash register.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb, to cashier is to dismiss an officer in disgrace, unrelated to the shop cashier.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishonourably discharged from military service, a punishment for officers.

parts.note: apprentices or learners in a trade making progress, and those who make things better

explanation.surface: A report that the labour force is thriving.
explanation.definitionFit: Apprentices learning a trade were once called this, and they also make things better.

parts.note: Reynard is the traditional name for the fox, and something for its hand is a glove: the foxglove gives a heart drug

explanation.surface: A fox's convenient cure.
explanation.walkthrough: Reynard is the fox of folk tales; 'handy' means worn on the hand, a glove, so the plant is the foxglove, whose drug treats the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart medicine extracted from foxglove leaves, also the plant's Latin genus name.

parts.note: the idiom of glaring at someone with hostile, piercing eyes, pictured as pointed blades

explanation.surface: Someone with keen good looks.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'look daggers' at someone is to glare at them angrily.
explanation.definitionFit: Short stabbing blades, and in the idiom 'look ...' a furious glare.

clue.text: Departs to return to the station

parts.note: dep. is the timetable abbreviation for departs

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the little word to is written backwards

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned

explanation.surface: A train leaves and then comes back to the station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns TO into OT, which follows DEP.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a bus or railway station, or a storage base.

explanation.surface: Inspectors wanted for bed components.
explanation.definitionFit: People who try things out are one sense; canopies over four-poster beds are the other.

parts.note: not a writer of leaflets but someone skilled at handing things out to others

explanation.surface: A specialist in printed leaflets.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who donates, handing things over freely, is a donor.

parts.note: the clergyman of the English song who changed his faith with each new monarch, from Bray in Berkshire; eminence also plays on a churchman's title

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a donkey's lofty bray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Vicar of Bray' is an English song about a cleric who kept his parish by switching faiths under each monarch; 'Bray' is the village, not a donkey's noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A parish priest, the turncoat cleric of the song being of Bray.

clue.text: Pardon, sir, are these for Iris?

indicators.note: the clue asks what the letters of Pardon, sir are when rearranged, the only signal for the mixing

parts.note: taken as written: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A polite question about whether some gift is meant for a girl named Iris.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris is the Greek goddess of the rainbow, which appears when sunlight passes through falling drops of water; the letters of PARDON SIR are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Falling water droplets split sunlight into the rainbow, Iris's sign.

clue.text: Though in debt the old boy's all dressed up!

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: being in the red means being in debt, so red stands for debt
OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: A man in debt still dresses smartly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts OB within RED; being 'in the red' is being in debt.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothed in robes, formally or grandly attired.

parts.note: a fixed reference level or starting point from which other measurements are taken

explanation.definitionFit: A fixed reference point or level from which measurements are reckoned, as in surveying.

parts.note: brand is an old word for a sword, so this is the king's legendary blade, not a trademark

explanation.surface: A trade name belonging to a man called Arthur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brand' is a poetic word for a sword, not a trade name.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur's legendary sword, drawn from the stone or given by the Lady of the Lake.

parts.note: taken as written
E is one of the musical notes A to G

explanation.surface: A tenor singer gives a group of people a note to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tenor' is not a singer but the general drift of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The tenor of a speech is its gist or main subject.

clue.text: What the poor wandering one surely did

definitions.text: What the poor wandering one surely did

parts.words: What the poor wandering one surely did
parts.note: a quotation from Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance: 'Poor wandering one, though thou hast surely ...'

explanation.surface: Musing on what a lost soul must have done.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pirates of Penzance Mabel sings 'Poor wand'ring one! Though thou hast surely strayed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who wanders has gone off course, roaming away from the right path.

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal
asks, used as a noun, are requests or questions

explanation.surface: A mother asking about silk fabrics.
explanation.definitionFit: Damask is a patterned silk fabric, first woven in Damascus.
